front: What does the one-period binomial model assume about the underlying?
back: Over one period the underlying moves to only two prices: up, S+ = S0·u, or down, S- = S0·d, with d < 1 + r < u.
h = (c+ - c-)/(S+ - S-): the units of the underlying held against one short call to make the position riskless.

front: Call value from the hedge ratio approach?
back: c0 = h·S0 - PV(h·S- - c-), where PV discounts at the one-period risk-free rate.

front: Risk-neutral probability of an up move?
back: π = (1 + r - d)/(u - d); the probability of a down move is 1 - π = (u - (1 + r))/(u - d).
c0 = [π·c+ + (1 - π)·c-]/(1 + r); the same method gives puts, using p+ and p-.

front: Why do real-world probabilities not affect the option price?
back: The option payoff is replicated by the underlying and a risk-free bond, so its price depends only on S0, the end states and r; beliefs and risk aversion are already in S0.
Otherwise one of the stock or the risk-free asset beats the other in both states, creating an arbitrage independent of any option.

front: How is an American option valued in a one-period tree?
back: Max of immediate exercise value and the European continuation value (discounted risk-neutral expected payoff).

front: When can early exercise of an American call be optimal?
back: Only when the underlying pays income (such as a dividend); a call on an asset with no cash flows is never exercised early.

front: How does the binomial model relate to put-call parity?
back: It satisfies parity automatically: c0 + K/(1 + r) = p0 + S0, since both are derived from no-arbitrage replication.
